en: A Philippine eagle's sharp, hooked beak acts as a wedge to tear apart the flesh of its prey.
The rough, textured footpads of a Philippine tarsier increase friction, allowing it to grip smooth tree branches securely.
The daily rising and falling of ocean tides in Manila Bay are caused by the moon's gravitational pull.
The dark volcanic sands along the beaches of Ilocos contain magnetite, a naturally magnetic iron ore mineral.
A sudden flash of lightning over the South China Sea is a massive discharge of built-up static electricity.
Sunlight refracts and reflects inside spherical raindrops after a tropical afternoon shower to create a visible rainbow.
The tiny Philippine pygmy bat emits high-frequency sound waves that bounce off trees to navigate dark caves.
The boiling mud pots and hot springs of Tiwi, Albay, are heated by thermal energy from underground magma.
The fast-flowing water of Maria Cristina Falls in Mindanao possesses kinetic energy used to spin hydroelectric turbines.
Fireflies along the Loboc River in Bohol convert stored chemical energy into glowing light energy to communicate.
The winding, zigzag path of Kennon Road in Baguio acts as a giant inclined plane for vehicles.
The smooth, streamlined body of an Irrawaddy dolphin in Guimaras reduces fluid friction as it swims.
